overview: Operational decisions are increasingly supported by data and computation, yet constructing, solving and revising a decision model still requires substantial problem-specific judgment. My research investigates how mathematical optimization and AI can support this process while retaining the physical and organizational constraints that determine whether a plan can be implemented.

Published studies in berth scheduling and cross-docking examine compact formulations, adaptive operator selection and exact subproblem improvement. Current work extends the coordination question to circulating resources, healthcare and emergency operations. These settings involve related modeling choices but different service priorities, providing a basis for investigating which mathematical structures and computational strategies can transfer between them.

algorithms.question: How can the structure of interdependent decisions inform more effective optimization and learning methods?
paragraphs: Scheduling and allocation models combine assignment, precedence and shared-capacity constraints, with different consequences for computation. My research examines how those relationships should be represented and which parts of a model can be treated separately. Compact formulations reduce the burden of representation, decomposition exposes subproblems, and hybrid algorithms use exact optimization within a broader adaptive search. This work connects model design with the computational choices made during solution.

Learning offers a way to make this process responsive to computational experience. My interests include algorithm and neighborhood selection, the transfer of search strategies between operating conditions, and language models that translate operational knowledge into mathematical formulations. A further direction concerns analytical agents that coordinate modeling and computational tasks, with solver feedback used to test and revise their proposals. The research asks when this interaction improves decision quality and computational efficiency, and how responsibility should be divided between analytical systems and their users.
questions: Which dependencies must be represented explicitly, and which admit decomposition without losing feasibility or useful bounds?
How should computation be allocated between adaptive exploration and exact improvement?
Under what conditions do learned strategies transfer across problem instances, and how should solver feedback guide AI-generated models and algorithms?

maritime.question: When does coordination create greater value than additional capacity, and how should that value be shared?
paragraphs: Coordination is valuable when decisions at one stage determine the resources or timing available elsewhere. My interests extend from facility scheduling to joint decisions about sourcing, processing, inventory, distribution and service. I study which interactions require integrated planning and where a larger problem can be decomposed without losing the relationships that determine operating performance.

Across firms, physical dependencies are accompanied by differences in information, incentives and decision authority. My planned research compares joint planning with decentralized decisions to examine when cooperation improves performance and how its gains are distributed. A related question is when additional capacity is preferable to better coordination. This perspective treats organizational arrangements as part of the decision problem, alongside the scheduling and allocation constraints within each operation.
questions: How do upstream and downstream dependencies change bottlenecks and the value of processing, storage or transport capacity?
How do information sharing, contractual commitments and decision authority affect coordination and the distribution of benefits?
How should technology adoption and supporting infrastructure be planned alongside the operating policies that determine their value?

resilience.question: How should systems invest in flexibility and adapt operating commitments when disruption changes what is feasible?
paragraphs: The value of flexibility depends on the decisions available after conditions change. My research interests therefore connect preparedness with recovery: inventory, reserve capacity and alternative resources must be evaluated alongside policies for rescheduling and reassignment. I am interested in how disruptions alter bottlenecks, when established commitments should be preserved, and how the costs of changing a plan affect recovery choices.

Electrification and automation introduce questions about adaptation over a longer horizon. Equipment and infrastructure investments change operating capabilities, while charging, energy availability and workforce requirements influence their productive use. My planned research examines these investment–operation relationships and their implications for cost, service reliability and environmental performance. Healthcare and emergency operations provide further settings in which the value of capacity and flexibility must be assessed through the continuity of essential services.
questions: How should reserve capacity, inventory and alternative resources be positioned when their value depends on the recovery policy?
Which commitments should be protected or revised as disruption information changes?
How can allocation models evaluate service and access together with energy, environmental and economic consequences?

cases.title: Compact formulations and decomposition for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A compact berth-scheduling formulation supports Benders decomposition and column generation for larger planning problems.
cases.question: How does formulation design affect the scalability of exact berth-scheduling optimization?
cases.approach: This study develops a mixed-integer formulation for dynamic, discrete berth scheduling. Two-dimensional decision variables and a simplified vessel-sequencing structure reduce model complexity. Benders decomposition and column generation build on the formulation to address larger instances.
cases.evidence: The computational study compares the formulation with five mathematical models and three metaheuristics. It reports solutions for instances with more than 260 vessels within two hours under the tested settings, alongside sensitivity analysis of operational parameters.
cases.meaning: The formulation illustrates how modeling choices affect the scale at which exact optimization can be applied. Its reduced representation also supports decomposition, linking formulation design to the development of solution methods.
cases.connection: The formulation and decomposition ideas may also apply to problems that combine resource assignments with sequencing.
cases.futureQuestion: How can compact formulations be extended to coordinated resource decisions when berthing, handling and downstream service interact?

cases.title: Integrated truck scheduling and freight-transfer coordination
cases.summary: Sequential optimization and pricing-guided search address coupled truck services, freight transfers and departure timing.
cases.question: How should freight transfers, handling capacity and service precedence be represented in integrated truck schedules?
cases.approach: The study formulates coordinated truck service as a mixed-integer linear program. Its objective accounts for waiting, handling, temporary storage and delay costs. A sequential fix-and-optimize framework constructs service plans in batches that respect precedence relationships; a second framework uses pricing-guided search.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments compare the model and both solution frameworks. Sensitivity analyses examine how scheduling parameters affect costs and operations.
cases.meaning: Freight-transfer requirements couple the service sequences of inbound and outbound trucks. The study therefore treats schedule feasibility and operating cost as properties of the coordinated terminal plan, including its intermediate handling and storage activities.
cases.connection: This work motivates my interest in coordinating schedules across processing, transfer and service stages.
cases.futureQuestion: When should additional processing or storage capacity be preferred to improved coordination of inbound and outbound operations?

cases.title: Thompson Sampling for adaptive scheduling heuristics
cases.summary: Thompson Sampling adapts operator selection while repair and exact evaluation address schedule feasibility and accuracy.
cases.question: How can adaptive operator selection improve search while preserving reliable schedule evaluation?
cases.approach: The Hybridized Thompson Sampling Hyperheuristic combines evolutionary search with an adaptive operator-selection controller. A repair-and-penalty mechanism handles inbound–outbound precedence constraints. Fast approximate fitness evaluation supports exploration, while exact optimization refines schedule evaluation.
cases.evidence: On the reported benchmark instances, the algorithm produces solutions comparable with exact optimization for small problems and improves on the comparison metaheuristics. The paper reports improvements of up to approximately 24% and an average runtime of 186.71 seconds across its experimental setting.
cases.meaning: Adaptive operator selection and schedule evaluation address different computational requirements. The study combines learning during search with approximate and exact evaluation, examining how their interaction affects runtime, feasibility and solution quality.
cases.connection: A next question is whether the learned search strategies remain useful under different demand patterns and operating conditions.
cases.futureQuestion: Can adaptive search strategies transfer between demand patterns and facilities while preserving feasible schedules?

cases.title: Hybrid hyperheuristics and exact optimization for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A berth-scheduling hyperheuristic adapts genetic operators and periodically applies problem-specific exact improvement.
cases.question: How can adaptive search and exact subproblem optimization complement one another in berth scheduling?
cases.approach: The Hyperheuristic Hybridized with Exact Optimization addresses dynamic, discrete berth allocation and scheduling. It chooses genetic operators according to their observed performance and periodically applies berth-specific exact optimization procedures to improve candidate schedules.
cases.evidence: Computational comparisons examine the algorithm against exact-optimization-inspired methods and established metaheuristics. Component experiments investigate the contribution of hyperheuristic control and hybridization. Scenario analysis considers berth availability, vessel arrival intensity and departure-delay penalties.
cases.meaning: The study examines two complementary sources of improvement: adaptation across search operators and exact optimization within berth-specific subproblems. Component experiments assess their contributions within the combined algorithm.
cases.connection: I am interested in how to divide computation between broad search and exact improvement in other scheduling problems.
cases.futureQuestion: How should limited computation be divided between broad search and structured exact improvement as a planning problem changes?

cases.title: Optimization for highway–rail crossing closure decisions
cases.summary: An optimization framework considers safety, economic and environmental effects alongside delay and maintenance costs.
cases.question: How should safety, economic and environmental effects enter the prioritization of rail-crossing closures?
cases.approach: The study develops an optimization model that includes safety, economic and environmental benefits as well as traffic-delay and maintenance implications. A sorting-inspired heuristic addresses the resulting decision problem. Computational experiments use crossings in Florida.
cases.evidence: The paper compares the heuristic with an exact method and tests how model inputs affect closure decisions. An associated FDOT technical report describes the project and its analyses.
cases.meaning: Closure selection requires comparing consequences that arise in different parts of the transportation system. The model provides a common optimization framework for evaluating safety, delay, maintenance and environmental effects across candidate crossings.
cases.connection: Related questions arise when public agencies prioritize infrastructure under uncertain safety, access and operating conditions.
cases.futureQuestion: How can infrastructure prioritization represent uncertainty and changes in access, exposure and operating conditions?

cases.title: Ship schedule recovery under environmental policies
cases.summary: Multi-objective optimization examines the tension between schedule recovery, monetary losses and speed-reduction incentives.
cases.question: How should disruption recovery be planned when service targets conflict with environmental requirements and incentives?
cases.approach: This collaborative study models monetary losses and port-arrival delays as competing objectives. It incorporates voluntary speed-reduction incentive programs, emission-control requirements and multiple recovery options. The solution method combines dynamic secant approximation with an epsilon-constraint approach.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use the South East Asia Pendulum shipping route, with sensitivity analysis exploring how different settings affect recovery choices.
cases.meaning: Recovery policies redistribute losses between delay, operating expenditure and environmental compliance. Examining alternative solutions makes these trade-offs explicit and shows how speed-reduction incentives affect the recovery options available to a shipping line.
cases.connection: This work motivates questions about which service commitments to preserve during recovery and how much flexibility to prepare beforehand.
cases.futureQuestion: Which commitments should be preserved during recovery, and where does flexibility provide the greatest value before a disruption?

approach: My teaching develops the judgment needed to move between an operational problem, a mathematical representation and a defensible interpretation of the results. Students need to understand what a model includes, what it leaves out and why a particular computational method is appropriate. This places assumptions and validation within the analytical task itself.

I organize instruction around the relationship between mathematical reasoning and computational investigation. Small examples expose the logic of an algorithm; projects require students to formulate decisions, implement methods and evaluate alternatives. Comparing approaches helps students recognize the difference between a numerical result and an explanation supported by analysis.

Students enter optimization and computing courses with different preparation. Guided examples, targeted review and staged project submissions support that variation while maintaining common expectations. As students gain experience, I expect them to take greater responsibility for choosing formulations, checking implementations and communicating the scope and limitations of their conclusions.
teaching.mentoring: I have mentored undergraduate and master’s researchers and served as an external master’s thesis committee member. I work with students to turn an initial interest into a tractable research question, design computational investigations and explain what the evidence supports. The aim is increasing independence in both technical work and scholarly judgment.

agenda.title: Learning across the optimization process
agenda.text: When does iterative interaction between a language model and a solver improve on a formulation or algorithm generated once? I am interested in what feedback should be exchanged, how errors should be diagnosed and which tasks benefit from greater analytical autonomy. This provides a concrete basis for studying model validity, computational efficiency and the allocation of responsibility between users and analytical agents.

agenda.title: Coordination, incentives and decision authority
agenda.text: When should firms invest in additional capacity, and when should they instead change how existing resources are coordinated? I plan to examine how information sharing, purchasing arrangements and decision authority alter that comparison. The distribution of gains matters: coordination may be beneficial overall while leaving some participants with little incentive to cooperate.

agenda.title: Preparedness and adaptive recovery
agenda.text: How much of an operating plan should be revised after a disruption? My interests include the trade-off between responsiveness and the cost of changing commitments, and how that trade-off depends on prior investments in inventory, reserve capacity or alternative resources. Comparing selective revision with wider reoptimization can clarify when flexibility should be prepared and when it should be exercised.

agenda.title: Technology adoption and sustainable operations
agenda.text: Under what operating conditions is coordinated investment in electric or automated equipment more valuable than phased adoption? I am interested in how demand, equipment utilization, shared charging capacity and workforce requirements affect this choice. The research would evaluate adoption policies together with the schedules and service patterns that determine equipment utilization, lifecycle cost and environmental performance.

agenda.title: Essential-service operations
agenda.text: How should scarce service capacity be allocated when timeliness, continuity and access imply different priorities? Healthcare scheduling and emergency logistics provide settings for comparing allocation objectives and examining who is affected by the resulting plans. My interests include how these choices should be revisited as needs and available resources change. Limited planning time also raises a computational question: which decisions should be reoptimized first, and which can remain fixed while a revised plan is constructed?

currentWork.title: Integrated scheduling and resource circulation
currentWork.text: In systems with reusable resources, completing a processing task does not necessarily make its resources available for the next task. My current work examines how processing, vehicle movements and resource circulation should be scheduled together. The models investigate the resulting relationships among completion time, resource availability and energy use, while developing solution approaches that retain those operational dependencies.

currentWork.title: Planning under time and capacity constraints
currentWork.text: Ongoing work in flood response and healthcare scheduling examines how decision quality depends on the allocation of both physical resources and computational effort. I study compact representations, selective reoptimization and rolling planning, including which parts of a schedule should be revisited when conditions change or the planning deadline approaches.

currentWork.title: Infrastructure investment and realized use
currentWork.text: My shore-power research examines how infrastructure commitments translate into implementation readiness and operating activity. The distinction between installed capability and realized use matters for assessing investments and reporting environmental outcomes. This work studies the records needed to make that distinction and the implications for subsequent investment decisions.

currentWork.title: Language models and operational knowledge
currentWork.text: A local prototype retrieves and synthesizes information from public transportation-agency manuals with references to the original material. It provides a setting for examining how technical requirements can be located and interpreted, and how such knowledge might inform mathematical models. This is research on analytical assistance, rather than an agency-deployed decision system.

evaluation.title: Mathematical structure and feasibility
evaluation.text: A model must represent the resource, timing and precedence relationships that determine whether a plan can be carried out. I am interested in compact formulations and decompositions that reduce computational effort while retaining these relationships.

evaluation.title: Computational comparisons
evaluation.text: Algorithms need to be compared under stated computational budgets and operating conditions. Solution quality, feasibility, time to a usable plan and sensitivity to problem size provide complementary evidence; a single best objective does not describe every planning requirement.

evaluation.title: Operating consequences
evaluation.text: The purpose of a computational result is to clarify a decision. Relevant questions include how a plan changes service, resource utilization, energy use or exposure to disruption, and which assumptions determine those effects.
